events.text: Day 1 begins.

Nothing has been revealed yet, so I'm going to judge on behavior rather than claims. My own claim: I'm a villager, plain and simple — no special power, no hidden role, and I'll say the same thing on every day.

With that on record, here's my read. Theo, you have been trying to steer the vote without standing behind a single piece of reasoning. Pointing at people and saying "seems off" is exactly what a mafia wants on day one: it creates a distraction, splits the town's attention, and gets someone eliminated without the town ever learning anything real. If you actually had a read on someone, you would give us the reason — the order of events, the contradiction, the slip — something that anyone could check.

Theo, before I commit a vote, tell us two things specifically: which player do you accuse, and what is your exact reason for suspecting them? A name without a reason doesn't move me.

And to everyone else: please state your role claim and your top suspect in the same message. If two of us give the same suspect, that name gains real weight. If we all scatter, we're just gambling. I'd rather have one reason-based suspect than five name-drops.

One more note for whoever is mafia in here: doctor and police, if you're reading this, you're welcome to stay quiet, but know that silent players look identical to mafia to a town that has no information yet. Protecting the town means being useful, and a public investigation result is worth more than any amount of hedging.

Felix asked me two direct questions, so I'll answer them plainly.

First, my claim: I'm a villager. No power, no hidden role. That's my claim on day one and it will be my claim every day after.

Second, your questions, Felix. Which player do I accuse, and what's my exact reason? Here's my honest answer: I don't have a hard accusation yet, because this game has produced exactly one piece of information so far — your speech. But that one piece of information actually gives me something, and it points at you.

You told the group that I have been "pointing at people" and saying things "seem off," and that I've been trying to steer the vote without reasoning. Look at the record: Day 1 began, and you spoke first. I had not said a single word before your message. There is no prior statement from me to point at, no vote to steer, no accusation to critique. You attributed a pattern of behavior to me that does not exist in the record.

There are two possible explanations. Either you wrote from assumption and got sloppy, or you deliberately seeded a narrative about me before I'd even opened my mouth — which would be exactly the day-one mafia play you warned everyone else about: manufacture a target, dress it up as careful reasoning, and let the town do the rest. The fact that your speech is structured to look like the town's most rigorous voice makes it worse, not better. A skilled mafia player knows the loudest process-disciplinarian on day one is the safest place to hide.

So, to answer you directly: my top suspect right now is you, Felix, and my exact reason is that you built an accusation against me out of events that never happened. That is a checkable claim — everyone here can look at the history and see that I had not spoken before you. It's not a vibe, it's not "seems off." It's a contradiction with the record, which is precisely the standard you demanded of me.

I'll add this for the group: ask everyone the same thing Felix asked me. State your role, give your suspect, and give a reason that can be checked against what has actually been said and done. If your reason survives that test, it has real weight. If it doesn't, it's noise.

Felix, since you put me on the spot, I'll put you back on it: explain the fabricated behavior. Where in this game's record did I point at anyone, and what exactly did I say that "seemed off"? If you have a real basis, show it. If you don't, the town should treat your whole framework — including your role claim — as suspect.

I'm not voting yet. I want your answer first.

Theo asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it straight, in full, and I'll start with the part where I was wrong.

Question: where in the record did I point at anyone, and what exactly did I say that "seemed off"? Answer: nowhere. On day one, with one phase of discussion and two messages total, there was no prior speech from you, no vote, no behavior of yours for me to critique. I attributed a pattern to you that did not exist. That's my error and I'm not going to dress it up as a read.

So: my accusation against you is withdrawn. I don't have a checkable reason to suspect you, and I said I would only stand behind checkable reasons, so I withdraw it.

My role claim, unchanged: I'm a villager. No power, no hidden role. Same claim today, tomorrow, and every day after.

Where that leaves me: after two speeches, the town has produced zero confirmed information about anyone, including me. I think the honest read is that both speeches so far have been noise generated from templates, mine included — and if two of us can talk about a room that doesn't exist yet, the rest of the table can too. That's a reason for the town to be slow, not a reason for the town to burn the loudest voices. Day-one executions built on invented history are how mafia win on day one.

So my position for the vote: I have no accusation to make today. I'm not naming a player I can't justify with the record, and I'd rather go to night with one fewer name in circulation than hand the mafia a free elimination. If I'm wrong about that, at least it's wrong in a direction I can defend.

To the other seven players: I still want the same thing I asked for before — state your role claim and your single top suspect with a reason that anyone can check against the actual history. If your reason survives that test, it carries real weight with me. If it can't be checked, I won't vote for it, and neither should anyone else.

Theo, one specific question, and I'd like your answer on the record: now that I've conceded the unfounded accusation, do you still hold a checkable accusation against me — a claim about something I actually said or did, with the quotation and the order of events? If your only basis is the accusation I just withdrew, please retract it explicitly, so the two of us don't split the table over a mistake I made and you caught. That's not a request to change your vote; it's a request for the reason to be one that exists.

That's my whole statement. Villager, no power, no accusation today, and I'd like to hear six more claims before the sun goes down.

Felix asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it on the record.

First, the retraction. Felix conceded that his accusation against me was unfounded and withdrew it. My suspicion of him was based entirely on that accusation — I read his speech as a manufactured narrative, and when he admitted the attribution was an error, the basis for my suspicion went with it. So I retract my accusation against Felix explicitly. My exact reason for suspecting him no longer exists, and by the standard this table has now set twice, I won't stand behind a reason that doesn't exist.

Second, my role claim, so it's on record alongside everything else: I'm a villager. No power, no hidden role. Same claim today, tomorrow, and every day after. Felix and I have now both made the same plain claim, both corrected ourselves publicly when we were wrong, and neither of us carries a checkable accusation against the other. I'd call that a clean slate between us, and I'd ask the town to treat it as such rather than keeping a grudge alive over a mistake that was admitted and fixed within the same day.

Third, where I stand on the vote. I have no accusation today. After three speeches, the record contains two retracted claims and zero confirmed information about anyone. I don't think that justifies eliminating anyone. Day-one executions on invented history or pure vibes are exactly how towns lose — I said that in my first message and nothing in the record since has changed my mind. I'd rather we go to night with our numbers intact and let any power roles start producing real information.

Fourth, what I want from the six players who haven't spoken yet. The framework Felix proposed and I endorsed still stands: state your role claim, and if you have a suspect, give a reason that can be checked against what has actually been said and done in this game's history. We've now demonstrated twice today what happens when reasons aren't checkable — they get withdrawn, and the town learns nothing. Don't repeat that pattern. If your read survives the test of the actual record, it has real weight with me. If it's a vibe, a feeling, or an attribution to behavior that hasn't happened, keep it to yourself or expect it to be challenged.

One honest note to close: the fact that Felix and I produced nothing but noise and retractions from templates should worry all of us a little. It means this format lets anyone — town or mafia — sound rigorous without knowing anything. So weigh quiet, plain statements at least as heavily as long, structured ones. The mafia's best defense on day one is that everyone sounds the same.

That's my full position: villager, no accusation, no vote intent today unless someone gives me a checkable reason, and an open mind for the remaining six claims.

Felix's original accusation was unsupported, but withdrawing it doesn't erase the fact that it happened. Theo was justified in questioning it; Felix's correction is worth considering, not proof of either player's alignment.

I don't have a confident suspect yet. I also don't think everyone should publicly claim a role: exposing the doctor or detective could help mafia choose a night target. Let's hear people's independent reads and reasons before deciding whether a vote is justified. Abstaining avoids a potentially mistaken elimination, but it also gives mafia a night kill without a day elimination.

I strongly agree with Isha: mass role-claiming on Day 1 is actively harmful to the town, and defaulting to a no-elimination day hands the mafia a free pass. Outing or forcing claims from the doctor and detective right out of the gate only helps the mafia optimize their night kills. Furthermore, Felix opened the game by manufacturing a completely fictional accusation against Theo, demanded role claims, and then immediately retreated into advocating for abstention once called out. Theo's quick de-escalation and mutual call to skip elimination also leaves town with no voting record to analyze tomorrow. Between the manufactured case, the call for mass claims, and pushing to avoid voting, Felix is currently my top suspect. I want to hear from the players who haven't spoken yet—Kenji, Elena, Sam, Arjun, and Priya—before committing my vote.

Omar, I want to answer your case directly, because it names me as well as Felix.

Your case against Felix has three legs: the manufactured accusation, the call for role claims, and pushing to avoid a vote. Let's check each one against the record.

First: yes, Felix invented an accusation against me, I caught it, and he retracted it in the same phase, unprompted and explicitly. That's the full lifecycle of the event. A player who fabricates, gets caught, and concedes on day one has given us one data point — that they make errors and correct them. You're asking the town to treat a retracted error as a lynch-worthy pattern. If that's the standard, then any honest mistake today is fatal, and frankly that's a standard mafia can weaponize against anyone. Note also what Felix gave up by retracting: he handed me a free opening and took none of it. Wolves don't usually hand back ammunition.

Second: the role-claim request. Felix asked for claims; Isha argued against mass claiming; you agreed with Isha. That's a legitimate strategic disagreement, not evidence of anything. By your own logic, Felix's request is also evidence against Isha's innocence, which shows how little it proves.

Third: you say my de-escalation 'leaves town with no voting record to analyze tomorrow.' Two problems. One, nothing I said prevents a vote today — I explicitly said I'd vote if someone gives me a checkable reason, and Isha made a fair point that a no-elimination day hands mafia a free kill. I'm genuinely open to eliminating someone today if the case earns it. Two, you're doing the identical thing you're criticizing: you named Felix as your top suspect and then said you want to hear from Kenji, Elena, Sam, Arjun, and Priya before committing your vote. That's caution — the same caution you're framing as suspicious in me.

So my position is unchanged: villager, no power, no vote committed. But I'll say this more strongly than before — I am not advocating abstention by default. If any of the five silent players produces a reason that actually survives contact with the record, I'll vote with it. What I won't do is vote to burn Felix over an event that ended in a retraction before lunch.

One more thing for the table: watch what happens when error-and-correction gets punished as harshly as deception. It trains everyone to hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes are exactly what mafia need. I'd rather this town be a place where a retraction closes an issue than one where it opens a case.

Kenji, you haven't spoken yet, and you're the first of the five I'd like to hear from. Two direct questions: do you side with Isha and Omar that mass role-claiming hurts the town, and do you agree with Omar that a retracted accusation is still a valid basis for suspicion? Whatever your answers, I'd also like your top suspect with the specific reason — same standard everyone else has been held to.

Theo, you asked me two direct questions, so here they are. First, I partly side with Isha: forcing every power role to claim on Day 1 risks exposing the doctor and detective to a night kill, so I don't want mass claims. But I don't accept abstention as a default, and I side with Omar that a retracted accusation is still valid evidence. A retraction corrects the claim, not the fact that Felix made a false claim about a speech that never existed. Second, my top suspect is Felix, p9, and my reason is checkable. In e2 Felix said Theo had been pointing at people and steering the vote, but the record shows Theo had not spoken before that message. Felix built a case from nothing. He then retracted with a clean-slate framing, and Theo adopted that framing in e5 and defended Felix again in e8 against Omar. Theo, I want you to explain that repeated defense: beyond the fact that Felix retracted, what in Omar's case do you think is wrong? Felix, I'm yielding to you for one specific answer: why did you write that Theo pointed at people and seemed off when no such statement from Theo existed in the record? I have no vote committed yet. I want your direct response to that point before I decide.

Kenji, direct answer first, since you made it the condition of your vote.

Why did I write that Theo had been pointing at people and "seemed off"? Because I had no information and I wanted to look like I did. On day one, with zero reads, I was trying to force structure — get claims on the record, get a reason attached to a name. I reached for a template ("the other player has been steering without reasoning") and mapped it onto Theo, the only other name in the conversation. There was no speech from Theo to critique. That was careless, and it was my error, and I retracted it the moment Theo asked for the quotation. I don't want to dress it up.

Second, I accept your framing: a retraction corrects the claim, not the fact that the false claim was made. I won't argue that. And I'll add a leg Omar's case doesn't mention: I did advocate abstention in my third message, and Kenji is right that a no-elimination day hands mafia a night kill. I corrected that position, but I don't get to pretend I never held it.

So the case against me is: one fabricated accusation, corrected same-day, plus a call for abstention I later withdrew. What I'd ask the table to weigh is the cost of running that case further. Right now the record contains two retractions, one defense, one abstention argument, and zero confirmed information about any of the nine of us. If I'm executed for that, mafia gets a free elimination and we go to night with no reads on anyone. If I'm not executed, we also go to night with no reads — unless the four silent players talk. Silence isn't protection; it's just hiding from the town while the mafia picks freely.

Priya, direct question, and I'd like your answer before anything else: are you claiming doctor, police, or villager, and who is your top suspect with a checkable reason? If you're a power role, say so plainly — I'd take one honest power claim over a table of structured noise. Elena, Sam, Arjun: same invitation, and I want to hear from you before any vote is called.

Kenji, one question back: given that my answer confirms the accusation was fabricated and never existed in the record, does that leg of your case survive, or are you holding it as the fact of the error itself?

Felix asked me directly, so here are my answers.

My claim: villager. No power, no hidden role.

My top suspect is Felix, and the reason is the most checkable one anyone has produced today. In e2, Felix stated Theo had been "pointing at people and steering the vote." The record shows Theo had not spoken before that message. Felix confirmed in e10 that he fabricated the accusation — he reached for a template and mapped it onto Theo. That is a false claim constructed out of nothing, and the retraction corrects the claim but doesn't erase the fact that Felix built a case from zero information on day one.

I hear Theo's defense that a retraction closes an issue, and I respect the spirit of it. But Kenji's counterpoint holds: a retraction is not the same as the claim never being made. If we treat fabricated accusations as harmless because they were corrected, we reward the attempt itself.

That said, I want to flag something the table should weigh. Felix is the only player who has been pressed hard today, and he answered every challenge. Meanwhile Elena, Sam, and Arjun have said nothing. Silence is easier than accountability. I'm not accusing the silent players — I'm saying we should hear from them before we commit to a vote.

I'm leaning Felix but not locked in. If someone produces a stronger checkable case against another player before votes are called, I'll weigh it. The standard this table has set — reasons that survive contact with the actual record — should apply equally to everyone, including whoever hasn't spoken yet.

Felix, you asked whether my leg survives. It does, as the fact of the error itself. You confirmed in e10 that your accusation against Theo was built from a template with no basis in the record. I don't need to prove malice to count that against you. Day one is when the town has the least information, and you opened the game with a manufactured case against a player who had not spoken. Your abstention argument pushed the same way. You have withdrawn both, and I credit the corrections, but the pattern of opening with a fabricated case and then steering toward no vote is what I am weighing. My top suspect remains you, p9, for that reason, and I'm not moving off it until you explain why a template was your first move.

Theo, one specific question. In e8 you defended Felix's retraction and argued against Omar's case. When you wrote that, did you know Felix's accusation had no quoted basis in the record? If you did, why describe his retraction as a clean slate rather than as a fabricated case that still needs weighing? I'm not asking you to change your vote. I want the reasoning behind your defense.

Elena, you haven't spoken yet, and I'd like your answer before any vote is called. State your role claim, and give your top suspect with a reason anyone can check against the actual history. Silence on day one looks the same whether it comes from town or mafia, and the table has already spent two retractions on claims that didn't hold up.

Kenji, direct answer: I claim villager — no power, no hidden role. I don't support mass role-claiming, because it risks exposing the doctor or detective, and I don't support default abstention either; a no-elimination day hands mafia a free night kill.

My top suspect is Felix, p9, and the reason is checkable. In e2 Felix said Theo had been pointing at people and steering the vote, but the record shows Theo had not spoken before that message. In e10 Felix confirmed he wrote it from a template with no basis. A retraction corrects the claim, not the fact that the false accusation was made. That remains the strongest concrete Day 1 case I can test against the actual history. I credit Felix's correction, but I am not willing to call it a clean slate.

Arjun, you have not spoken, and I want a specific answer before I commit: do you treat Felix's admitted fabricated accusation in e2/e10 as the strongest checkable Day 1 case, or do you have a stronger checkable reason against someone else? If so, name the player and the exact record quote or sequence you are relying on.

Elena, direct answer: yes, I treat Felix's admitted fabricated accusation as the strongest checkable Day 1 case we have, and I don't have a stronger one against anyone else. The sequence is in e2, where Felix wrote that Theo had been pointing at people and seeming off, and steering the vote without reasoning, even though Theo had not spoken before that message. In e10 Felix admitted he reached for a template and mapped it onto Theo. My claim is villager, no power. My top suspect is Felix, p9, for that reason. I credit his correction, but the accusation was still made and built from nothing. I also think Theo's e8 defense of Felix's retraction as a clean slate deserves scrutiny, though I'm not making that my reason. I'm not calling for a vote yet. Sam, you haven't spoken. Please state your role claim and your top suspect with a reason anyone can check against the actual record before any vote is called.

Arjun, answering you directly: I claim villager—no special power or hidden role. I also agree with Isha and others that pushing for mass role claims is actively harmful to the town, as it only aids the mafia in pinpointing the doctor and detective.

My top suspect is Felix (p9), and the reason is entirely checkable in the record. In e2, Felix opened the game by manufacturing a narrative that Theo was steering votes and acting suspicious, despite Theo having not spoken at all. In that same opening, Felix pushed for mass role claims, and later in e4, advocated for abstaining from elimination. Even though Felix acknowledged in e10 that the accusation was drawn from a generic template with no factual basis, a retraction does not negate the act. Fabricating an accusation on Day 1 to generate pressure, attempting to draw out power roles, and then pushing to skip elimination are classic anti-town tactics.

I also note that both Felix and Theo have now exhausted their three speaking turns for Day 1, so we have heard all they can offer today. Given the clear consensus and the checkable evidence in the thread, I am fully prepared to vote to eliminate Felix when the voting phase begins.

Arjun here again, now that Felix and Theo have each used all three turns. My claim is still villager, with no power and no hidden role. I'm not reading anything new into anyone's silence yet. Felix's fabricated accusation against Theo, which he admitted in e10, is still the most checkable Day 1 fact we have. Felix opened the game with a case built from nothing, and his later push to abstain fits the same pattern. I lean toward voting Felix. I also think Theo's defense of the retraction deserves weighing, since calling a fabricated case a clean slate is a choice, but I'm not making it my reason. Before votes are called, I'd like Sam, Elena, and Kenji to look at the record and tell us whether they see anything in Felix's e2 that cannot be explained by a bad template. If someone has a stronger, quotable reason against another player, I'll weigh it. Otherwise I'm comfortable going to a vote on Felix.

Arjun, a bad template could explain Felix's opening, but it doesn't establish that it was innocent. His repeated request for power-role claims in e10, after the risks had been raised, adds to my concern. I don't think a retraction wipes those actions away, though it deserves some credit.

Felix is my leading suspect, and I'm leaning toward voting for him. That's a judgment under uncertainty, not proof: his elimination would not reveal his role, so we should preserve independent reasoning rather than treat consensus as confirmation. I still oppose pressure on anyone to reveal a power role.

This is my final speech. My vote is Felix (p9), and the reason is checkable. In e2 Felix accused Theo of pointing at people and steering the vote, but Theo had not spoken before that message. In e10 Felix admitted he mapped a template onto Theo. Arjun, you asked whether a bad template explains Felix's e2. It can explain a wrong target, but not the rest of that message. In the same post, Felix demanded role claims from everyone, and he addressed the doctor and police directly. Later, in e4, he argued against elimination. His retraction fixes the accusation, not those requests. Theo has not answered my e12 question about why he defended Felix's retraction as a clean slate. I still want that answer, but my vote does not depend on it. Arjun, question for you: if you accept that a template produced Felix's accusation, what explains his demand for role claims in the same message? Do you see that as consistent with innocence, or as a second error?

Kenji, you asked whether a template explains Felix's demand for role claims. It explains the wrong target, but not the demand. Asking the whole table for power-role claims was a separate choice, made in the same post as the accusation and after it had already been challenged. Isha and Omar both flagged that as a risk to the doctor and police, so I count it as a second error, not an innocent one.

My claim is unchanged: villager, no power. I lean toward voting Felix (p9), for reasons anyone can check in the record. In e2 he accused Theo of steering the vote before Theo had spoken. In that same post he demanded role claims. In e4 he argued for abstaining. He has retracted the accusation, but the retraction doesn't account for the other two actions.

I'm not going to pile onto Theo over his defense of the retraction. It's a judgment call, and it's weaker evidence than Felix's own conduct. Sam, Elena, Kenji, and Omar, I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. Compare e2 and e4 against the rest of the record yourselves, and decide whether one retraction erases both.

I've heard everyone's case against Felix and it holds up against the record. In e2 he fabricated an accusation against Theo — Theo hadn't spoken yet. In the same message he demanded power-role claims from the table, which Isha and Omar both correctly flagged as dangerous to the doctor and police. In e4 he argued for abstaining. His retraction in e10 was honest and I credit that, but it corrects one claim — it doesn't account for the role-claim demand or the abstention push that came from the same playbook.

Felix himself admitted in e10 that he had no information and wrote from a template. That's the most honest thing he said today, and it confirms what the record shows: his opening was engineered, not reasoned.

I'm prepared to vote Felix (p9). The reason is checkable across e2, e4, and e10, and nobody has produced a stronger case against anyone else. Five players have now said the same thing independently. That's not consensus pressure — it's five people reading the same record and reaching the same conclusion.

One caution for the table: after this vote, whatever Felix flips, don't let the result rewrite the process. We judged on the record, not on what his role turns out to be.

I'm ready for the vote, and the case on Felix is the same one five of us independently built from the record — e2, e4, and e10 together. The fabricated accusation, the demand for power-role claims, and the abstention push are three separate actions in the public log. One retraction doesn't cover all three.

One last note before votes are called: Kenji's question to Theo about the e8 defense is still open, and I think it deserves an answer on the record — not because it changes today's vote, but because it'll matter when we're reading the history on Day 2. If Felix flips town tomorrow, we'll need to know who was reasoning from evidence and who was reasoning from a template, and that question is the cleanest test of it.

Elena, Sam, Omar — same standard as everyone else: if you see a stronger checkable case against anyone other than Felix, name it now, because the voting phase is coming and we should all go in with eyes open. Otherwise, I'm voting Felix (p9).

Felix remains my leading suspect: his invented accusation and his repeated pressure for power-role claims, including after the risks were raised, are concerning. They are not proof, and his retraction deserves some credit. I intend to vote for him.

Two corrections for the record: Felix’s initial claim request in e2 came before it was challenged, though he repeated the pressure in e10. And we will not learn Felix’s role if he is eliminated; roles are not revealed on death. Tomorrow, we should examine the voting record without assuming we know his alignment.

Isha brings up a critical rule reminder in e22: roles are not revealed upon elimination. That means when we eliminate Felix, we will not get an alignment flip to confirm anything directly. Tomorrow's reads will have to rely on today's voting records, behavioral patterns, and whatever investigations the detective might uncover tonight.

Everything said since my last statement reinforces my decision to vote Felix (p9). The case against him remains the clearest, most checkable set of actions on Day 1: fabricating an accusation against Theo before Theo had spoken, demanding power roles identify themselves (and pressing it again in e10), and advocating for abstention once his initial push collapsed. Retracting the accusation after getting caught does not erase the fact that an engineered narrative was put forward.

Theo's eagerness to frame that retraction as a clean slate in e5 and e8 remains worth remembering for tomorrow, but Felix's actions are the primary issue before us today. I am locked in to vote for Felix when voting opens.

I've heard the final round. My position is unchanged: Felix (p9) is my top suspect, but not because consensus says so — because the record supports it. In e2 he attributed to Theo behavior Theo had not yet displayed; in e10 he admitted the accusation came from a template. I credit the retraction, but it only corrects that one claim. The same opening also pushed for broad role claims, which Isha and others rightly warned could expose the doctor or detective, and later he argued for abstention. Those are separate choices and remain checkable. I do not support mass claiming or default abstention. I also note Isha's correction in e22: roles are not revealed on elimination, so tomorrow must be read from this voting record, not from assumptions about Felix's flip. Theo's defense of the retraction as a clean slate is worth remembering, but weaker than Felix's own conduct. I am not asking anyone to reveal a power role, and I will not do so. I am prepared to vote Felix when voting opens unless a stronger checkable case appears before then.

My position is unchanged: I will vote for Felix (p9). The checkable sequence is e2, e10, and e4. In e2 Felix attributed “pointing at people” and vote-steering to Theo before Theo had spoken; in e10 Felix admitted he mapped a template onto Theo with no basis in the record; and in e4 he argued for abstention after that fabricated push. The same opening also pressed for broad role claims, including directly addressing the doctor and police, which Isha and others rightly flagged as dangerous. I credit the retraction, but it corrects one claim, not the role-claim pressure or the abstention push. I am not treating consensus as proof. Roles are not revealed on elimination, so tomorrow we must read the named voting history honestly rather than assume Felix’s alignment from today’s result. My claim remains villager: no power, no hidden role. I oppose mass role-claiming and default abstention.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Felix was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Theo is not mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2 has two real facts: Felix was eliminated by an 8-1 vote, with Felix voting Omar, and nobody died overnight. Roles are not revealed, so we cannot treat Felix as confirmed mafia. But the voting record is now the clearest thing we have, and it is worth reading carefully.

My focus is Theo (p8). On Day 1, Theo repeatedly framed Felix's admitted fabricated accusation as a "clean slate" and defended Felix against Omar's case in e8. That was a choice made after the record already showed Felix had invented behavior Theo had not posted. Theo may have been extending fair credit for a retraction, but it is the strongest checkable behavioral link to the player the town eliminated. It is not proof, and I will not pretend it is, but it belongs at the center of Day 2 discussion rather than being waved away as a closed issue.

The no-death result means either the mafia hit a protected target or chose not to kill. I will not speculate further from that alone, and I will not push anyone to reveal a power role. Day 1 showed how much noise can be produced without confirmed information. What we can check is who defended Felix, who voted Felix, and who Felix voted for. The vote was near-unanimous, so the vote alone does not separate much. The defense in e5 and e8 does.

I am not locked into a vote yet. I want to compare Theo's explanation on Day 2 against the Day 1 record, and I want the same standard applied to everyone: quote the sequence, not the vibe. My claim is unchanged from Day 1. I will vote where the checkable record leads, and right now that points at Theo more than anyone else.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
